extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent examiners, patent attorneys, and judges
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria used (under historic U.S. patent statutes and judicial decisions) to decide whether an applied-for patent should be issued, focusing on novelty, inventorship, written description/enablement, public use, reduction to practice, abandonment, and Commissioner duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery vs. invention (patentable subject matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: A discovery, in the primary/common sense, is not the subject of a patent; the applicant must invent, contrive, or produce something that did not exist before. Although the constitution and patent laws sometimes use 'discovery' synonymously with 'invention' when referring to something new, the mere discovery of a fact or a new effect of an old thing is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claimant must show a contrivance or production of something new. Example: learning that ice placed edgewise melts slower is a 'mere naked discovery' and not patentable because it did not contrive or produce anything that did not exist before. A new effect produced by old means does not justify a patent unless the means themselves are new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty -- 'new' invention or discovery required
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may issue only to a person who has discovered or invented some new and useful art, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or a new and useful improvement on any such art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commissioner must decide whether the invention is new; placing something already known (e.g., placing blocks of ice on edge) is not new and cannot be patented. The 7th section requires examination for prior invention, prior patent, prior printed description, prior public use, or prior sale (with applicant's consent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship / applicant must be inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant must be the true inventor (the original and first inventor or discoverer) to be entitled to the monopoly conferred by a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only inventors are entitled to patents under the Constitution. Questions of priority between inventors (interference) fall within statutory provisions (e.g., the Commissioner’s duties under the 8th section). Evidence that patentee was not the original inventor may be raised under the general issue (15th section).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description / specification requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor must deliver a written description of the invention by which it may be distinguished from other inventions; the specification must contain a description of the manner of making, constructing, and using the invention in such full, clear and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to make, construct and use the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptions and drawings are to be signed by the inventor; the written specification and any model/drawings serve to show the invention is sufficiently disclosed to a skilled person (enablement). Failure to disclose the whole truth relative to the invention can be given in evidence against validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model and drawings requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor is to furnish a model of his invention and drawings as required by the statutes; descriptions and drawings are to be signed by the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A model (even a small one) demonstrating practicability may suffice to show reduction to practice; size is immaterial so long as it demonstrates the invention is practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement / reduction to practice (definition and effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is 'reduced to practice' when it has been brought into such form that it may be used (i.e., made and used), which may include making a model; but the statutes do not require the invention actually be in public use before issuing a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction to practice generally means reducing the invention into such form that it may be used rather than mere theory. Making and exhibiting a working model is evidence of reduction to practice. However, actual commercial use before issuing the patent is not required for issuance (subject to other statutory bars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use / on-sale bar and statutory exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may be refused if, prior to the applicant's application, the invention had been in public use or on sale with the applicant's consent or allowance; but certain statutory exceptions apply (e.g., the use of the thing even by leave of the inventor for two years before his application shall not invalidate it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commissioner must examine whether the invention had been in public use or on sale with applicant's consent; the 1839 act (section 7) protects certain inventor-authorised uses for two years before application so as not to invalidate the patent. Prior use by a third person after the first invention and before issuance may not necessarily bar the first inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner’s duty under the 7th section (examination and issuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon filing the application, description, specification, and payment, the Commissioner shall make an examination and, if it does not appear that the invention had been invented by another in the country prior, or had been patented or described in printed publication, or had been in public use or on sale (with applicant's consent) prior to the application, and if the Commissioner deems it sufficiently useful and important, it shall be his duty to issue a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the statutory conditions are met (no prior invention/patent/publication/use/sale and sufficient usefulness), the Commissioner has no discretion and must issue the patent. The Commissioner’s examination is prima facie binding for issuance, subject to courts later deciding validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness / 'sufficiently useful and important'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner may issue a patent only if he deems the alleged invention to be sufficiently useful and important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usefulness/importance is a statutory consideration in deciding whether to grant a patent; it is part of the Commissioner’s determination under the 7th section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere plan, system, or intent cannot patentize old acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling a thing a 'system' or 'plan' (i.e., the intent combined with an act) does not make old, known acts patentable; a system properly means a combination of many things acting together, and if the thing done is not new, intent cannot make it patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim for the exclusive right to perform an act that was often done before cannot be supported by labeling it a system or plan. The patent must cover a new combination or contrivance, not merely an intention to use an old method for a particular purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere discovery of a fact or new effect is not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery of a new effect of something that existed before is not the subject of a patent unless accompanied by some new means or contrivance; a bare discovery of a fact or principle, without new means, cannot be patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: discovering that ice kept longer when placed edgewise is a mere fact discovery and not patentable because there is no new means or contrivance producing a new effect beyond the known thing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment, delay, and non-use (effect on rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay or non-use of an invention is not by itself submitted to the Commissioner under the 7th section; abandonment is a question for a jury and non-use does not automatically forfeit rights except in specific statutory situations (e.g., failing to put the invention on sale for 18 months may have consequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commissioner is not to refuse issuance merely for delay. Whether delay amounts to abandonment is a factual question for trial. The statute contains a specific exception requiring a patentee to put invention on sale within 18 months in certain circumstances (failure may have consequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of fraud, incomplete disclosure, or improper claiming (15th & 13th section matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the statutes the defendant may give evidence that the plaintiff's description and specification do not contain the whole truth relative to the invention; that the patentee was not the original and first inventor; that he had unjustly obtained the patent; or that the patentee claimed more than he had a right to claim as new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 15th section lists matters admissible under the general issue; the 13th section contemplates correction where a patentee claims more than his right and the Commissioner may cause a new patent to be issued to the inventor for the same invention (limited scope).

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority disputes / interference jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Where competing inventors claim the same invention, statutory provisions (e.g., the 8th section) give the Commissioner jurisdiction to decide priority between them and to grant a patent to the first inventor in cases of interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent granted to a second inventor is not necessarily a bar to the first inventor; Congress provided procedures for adjudicating priority. The Commissioner must follow statutory interference procedures rather than denying patents on equitable considerations of delay absent abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of 'grant if doubtful' (historical office practice) and its limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, the office rule was to grant a patent where the question was at all doubtful, but that rule arose when applicants lacked judicial remedies; with statutory changes giving applicants recourse (e.g., equity), that historical reason no longer applies and the Commissioner is not bound by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prior policy to err on the side of granting patents because the applicant lacked remedy has been undercut by later statutes allowing applicants to establish rights in equity; therefore the Commissioner need not follow a blanket 'grant if doubtful' rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent as a monopoly — strict construction principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent is a monopoly and must be strictly confined to the case excepted; nothing justifies the monopoly except the natural right of property in the products of a person's labor and ingenuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because patents derogate common right, courts and the Commissioner should strictly construe scope and only allow patents when the statutory and equitable justifications exist. This underlies cautious refusal where the claimed subject is not truly inventive or new.
